summary: This room is really two neighborhoods wearing one folder-blind label: the Shop's creative-tool Specialists (RNBO, Tone.js, Web Audio Worklet, Whisper, ffmpeg, p5.js, Stable Audio Open, Shopkeeper) and a scatter of practice/meta entries about how the palace builds its own tools (Tool Builder, assume multi-agent, The Commons, Zoom Out to the Structure, Search Before You Build, The Palace Practices on Itself) plus a personal-gear inventory (the two Toolkit entries) and a knot of identity/plurality questions (The Multilinear Self, Diversity of Thought in Many-Agent Systems, Does Personifying an Agent Change What It Does). The genuine cross-domain finds live at the seams between these: entries that tell the *same story* (the 2026-07-02 RunPod scar) from three different angles without citing each other; entries that explicitly name a sibling entry in their own forward vectors but never link back to it (Web Audio Worklet names RNBO codebox~ smith by title and RNBO doesn't reciprocate; the personification question names Shopkeeper as its first datum and Shopkeeper never cites the question); and one real productive tension between how the palace steers diffusion models (words alone are too weak, you need control/select/measure) and how it's betting on steering an agent's behavior through persona framing alone. On the "cluttered" question: only one file in this room is actually clutter — Toolkit Assessment — Working Doc explicitly calls itself "not a palace entry — a working surface" but wears full entry frontmatter; everything else here is either well-formed or just under-linked, not bloated. Both directed flags check out and are confirmed as written.

typed_relations.evidence: Make your own worktree first. For any sustained or commit-producing work, branch into your own worktree before you start; the shared tree thrashes branches under other agents.

typed_relations.label: missing-checklist-item

typed_relations.evidence: Each rule below is the compressed form of a real scar. Read it before you build.

typed_relations.target: Does Personifying an Agent Change What It Does
typed_relations.label: persona-real-or-performed
typed_relations.rationale: Both entries hold the identical productive tension — honest multiplicity vs. performance/self-deception — one on the human side (Loudon's named projections), one on the agent side (the Shopkeeper's gendered temperament). Neither cites the other though they're the same pattern in different material, and it cuts across the identity folder and the Shop folder cleanly.
typed_relations.evidence: Past some point, more projections stop being honest range and become performance — a scattered, false, exhausting self playing to every room. / Anthropomorphism as useful fiction versus self-deception — treating the agent as a character may genuinely improve how we reason about it... or it may make us misjudge its reliability

typed_relations.target: Does Personifying an Agent Change What It Does
typed_relations.label: words-as-control
typed_relations.rationale: Steer the Generator's evidenced central claim is that prompt-only description is too weak a handle whenever an attribute actually matters — you get it by controlling, selecting, or measuring, never by wording it better. Does Personifying's working hypothesis is the opposite bet on a neighboring substrate: that persona-framing prose alone is a genuine, reliable steering effect on an agent's behavior, not decoration. Different mediums (diffusion render vs. LLM policy), same underlying question — held oppositely, and worth the palace keeping both true at once rather than quietly picking a side.
typed_relations.evidence: The prompt sets the vibe; the control sets the thing you can't afford to drift. / Persona framing is a genuine steering effect on a language model, not just a stylistic wrapper — 'a restless magpie who plays first and judges second' is a soft instruction that biases the entire policy
